sections.COMMENTS:
This Composite Source straddles the marine area between the termination of the Italian peninsula in Calabria and the northeastern tip of Sicily, including the western flank of the Aspromonte massif (with the city of Reggio Calabria) and the east-facing slope of the Peloritani Mts. (with the city of Messina). This source is a low-angle, ESE-dipping, fault located at the southwestern end of the extensional axis that runs along the southern Apennines.
Historical catalogues (Boschi et al., 2000; Gruppo di Lavoro CPTI, 2004; Guidoboni et al., 2007) show a remarkable concentration of damaging earthquakes in the the area. In particular, this region has been struck by the 28 December 1908 Messina (Calabria Meridionale) earthquake (Mw 7.2), one of the most catastrophic events of the Italian seismic history. The area has been affected by large earthquakes also in 91 B.C. (Mw 6.3, Reggio Calabria), 374 A.D. (Mw 6.3, Reggio Calabria), and on 31 August 853 (Mw 6.3, Messina), 25 February 1509 (Mw 5.6, Calabria Meridionale), 6 February 1783 (Mw 5.9, Calabria Meridionale).
The Messina Straits is a remarkably puzzling area. A vast literature has been produced over the decades, particulary in light of the catastrophic 1908 earthquake, to investigate its complex geology and tectonics. Data are abundant, like the various interpretations - sometimes contrasting with one another. There exist two main interpretations for the source of the 1908 earthquake in the framework of the recent evolution of the Messina Straits.
One view, based on structural geology and geomorphic observations, indicates the existence of a graben including three main fault sets trending NE-SW, NW-SE, and E-W. In this interpretation, the fault responsible for the 1908 earthquake would be a high-angle, NE-trending, W-dipping fault that comes to the surface on the Calabrian side of the Straits east of Reggio Calabria. Various lines of evidence, however, and in particular 1) the size of the causative fault for a Mw>7.0 earthquake, 2) the known depth of the seismogenic layer, and 3) the absence of reported coseismic surface faulting (despite the enormous amount of fieldwork by numerous and diverse teams over the years), all suggest that this hypothesis is unrealistic.
The second view proposes that the source of the earthquake is a low-angle blind fault dipping toward the ESE. This interpretation agrees well with available instrumental data (coseismic elevation changes) and suits convincingly the pattern of long-term deformation shown by the geologic and geomorphic observations.
A large portion of this Source has been associated with the 1908 earthquake. For an in-depth analysis of seismogenic processes in this region, the reader may refer to the relevant Individual Source in this Database.
The strike of the Source was based on the model derived from instrumental data, from the orientation of regional extension, on the distribution of the most recent paleo-shorelines, and on the local drainage pattern. Also the dip was based on instrumental data and on geological and geometrical considerations. Rake is indicative of almost pure normal faulting, based on geological and seismological data. The minimum and maximum depth were based on geological and seismological data. The slip rate was based on seismological data.

pictures.c: Summary of  fault models proposed by various investigators for the 1908 earthquake based on seismological, geodetic, geologic and macroseismic observations (from Valensiseand Pantosti [1992]).

Geological sketch of the Messina Straits area, interpreted as a graben structure formed by the intersection of various smaller normal faulting systems with a west-dipping master fault on the Calabrian side (from Ghisetti [1984]).

Summary of geologic and geomorphic observations for Messina Straits. The drainage pattern, the dip of marine terraces and the attitude of young sediments describe subsident areas due to ongoing slip on buried normal faults (from Burrato et al. [1999]).
Vertical displacement induced by the 1908 Messina Straits earthquake compared with selected geologic and geomorphic features (from Cucci et al. [1996]).
Schematic section of the fault systems in the general context of the active Calabrian W-dipping subduction (from Tiberti et al. [2017]).

pictures.c: Overview of the Calabrian sources. Notice that 1. the main normal faults lie antithetic to the subduction plane and host the largest earthquakes, and 2. between 1783 and 1908 large earthquakes ruptured the western extensional domain of the Southern Calabria (from Tiberti et al. [2017]).
